source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Signs of Strength in a Trend

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; sides field states mirrored/same

candidates.name: TrendBarClassification
candidates.quote: Most of the bars are trend bars in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: Primitive: the current bar is a bull trend bar -- its body covers most of the bar's high-low range and it closed up.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used to build other signs)

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic on open/high/low/close

notes: Brooks gives no numeric fraction here; reused as the base for several other signs in this chapter.

candidates.name: SmallOrNoTailBar
candidates.quote: There are bars with no tails or small tails in either direction, indicating urgency.
candidates.description: Primitive: both wicks of the current bar are small relative to its range -- neither the top tail nor the bottom tail exceeds a fraction of the bar's high-low range.
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - MaxList(open[0], close[0])) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (MinList(open[0], close[0]) - low[0]) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: single-bar arithmetic

notes: Brooks gives no numeric tail fraction; 0.1 is a reading of 'small'.

candidates.name: FractionOfBarsAreTrendBars
candidates.quote: Most of the bars are trend bars in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: Sign-of-strength context filter: over the last N bars, at least a fraction F of them are bull trend bars (T19-01) -- a sign the up move is strong and should be favored for with-trend entries.
candidates.pseudocode: countTrendBars(close, open, high, low, lookback, bodyFraction) >= minFraction * lookback
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: window loop counting a per-bar classification over N bars

candidates.name: LittleBodyOverlapBetweenBars
candidates.quote: There is very little overlap of the bodies of consecutive bars. For example, in a bull spike, many bars have lows that are at or just one tick below the closes of the prior bar.
candidates.description: This bar's low sits at or only a small number of ticks below the prior bar's close (bull trend) -- almost no give-back into the prior bar's body, a sign traders are buying aggressively.

complexity.reason: two-bar comparison on fixed offsets

notes: overlapTicks is expressed in price points/ticks; instrument-specific.

candidates.name: BodyGapBetweenBars
candidates.quote: Occasionally, there are gaps between the bodies (for example, the open of a bar might be above the close of the prior bar in a bull trend).
candidates.description: This bar's open trades beyond (above, in a bull trend) the prior bar's close -- a body gap, a strong sign of urgency.

complexity.reason: two-bar comparison

candidates.name: MicroMeasuringGap
candidates.quote: if the low of the bar after a strong bull trend bar in a bull trend is at or above the high of the bar before the trend bar, this is a gap and a breakout test and a sign of strength.
candidates.description: Across three consecutive bars where the middle bar is a strong bull trend bar, the bar after it never trades back into the range of the bar before it -- a micro measuring gap and sign of strength.
candidates.pseudocode: close[1] > open[1] && (close[1] - open[1]) >= bodyFraction * (high[1] - low[1]) && low[0] >= high[2]

complexity.reason: fixed three-bar-offset arithmetic combining a bar classification with a gap test

candidates.name: MeasuringGapHoldsBreakout
candidates.quote: Measuring gaps occur where the breakout test does not overlap the breakout point. For example, the pullback from a bull breakout does not drop below the high of the bar where the breakout occurred.
candidates.description: Since a designated breakout bar, no later pullback low has traded back below that breakout bar's high (bull case) -- confirms the breakout is holding and the trend is strong.

complexity.reason: requires first identifying and persisting a 'breakout bar' from an earlier, separately-defined breakout event, then tracking its high/low as state across all later bars

notes: 'Breakout bar' identification itself is out of scope for this candidate; assumed available as persisted state.

candidates.name: FewLargeBars
candidates.quote: Not many large bars appear (not even large trend bars).
candidates.description: This bar's range is not much larger than the recent average bar range -- the trend lacks big or climactic bars, a sign of an orderly, strong trend.

complexity.reason: window average of bar range compared with a multiple

notes: Roughly the negation of BarRangeAboveStd but expressed as a plain multiple of the mean rather than a standard-deviation band.

candidates.name: SmallSidewaysPullbacks
candidates.quote: There are small, infrequent, and mostly sideways pullbacks. For example, if the Emini's average range is 12 points, the pullbacks will all likely be less than three or four points.
candidates.description: The depth of the current pullback (retracement from the most recent swing high, in a bull trend) stays below a fraction of the average bar range -- a sign the trend is strong.

complexity.reason: requires a persisted 'most recent swing high' pivot value alongside a window average

candidates.name: NoPullbackForNBars
candidates.quote: the market will often go for five or more bars without a pullback.
candidates.description: None of the last N bars was a countertrend (bear) bar in a bull trend -- the trend has run N straight bars with no pullback at all.

complexity.reason: window loop over a per-bar open/close comparison

notes: Different from ConsecutiveUpBars: this only requires the ABSENCE of an opposite-direction bar, not that every bar close above its own open.

candidates.name: NoConsecutiveCloseAcrossEma
candidates.quote: No two consecutive trend bar closes occur on the opposite side of the moving average.
candidates.description: The last two closes are not BOTH on the wrong side of the moving average for the trend direction (e.g., in a bull trend, not two closes in a row below the EMA) -- a sign of a strong, one-sided trend.

complexity.reason: needs an EMA value and a two-bar look-back against it

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBar
candidates.quote: There is a sequence of 20 moving average gap bars (20 or more consecutive bars that do not touch the moving average, discussed in book 2).
candidates.description: Primitive: this bar's entire range stays clear of the moving average -- in a bull trend, the bar's low is above the EMA.

complexity.reason: requires an EMA value per bar

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBarStreak
candidates.quote: There is a sequence of 20 moving average gap bars ... Whenever the market stays away from the moving average for 20 bars or more (a 20 gap bar buy setup), the trend is very strong and the odds are high that there will be buyers at the moving average.
candidates.description: At least N consecutive bars have not touched the moving average -- a strong-trend sign that also sets up buying the eventual first pullback into the EMA (the '20 gap bar' setup).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter feeding a later EMA-touch entry, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: cross-bar persisted streak counter built on an EMA-based primitive

candidates.name: BigGapOpen
candidates.quote: There is a big gap opening on the day. ... the 5 minute Emini gapped up 11 points, which is huge, and the first bar was a bull trend bar.
candidates.description: The session's opening price gaps beyond a threshold distance from the prior session's close -- a sign the day may become a strong trend day.

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and the prior session's closing price carried as state

notes: gapThreshold is instrument-specific (points), Brooks's 11-point Emini example is not a stated rule value.

candidates.name: GapDoesNotReverseEarly
candidates.quote: Large gaps that don't reverse early usually mark the start of a strong trend for the day and the day often closes at or near the high (or low, in a bear).
candidates.description: After a big gap up (T19-14), price has not traded back down through the prior session's close within the first N bars of the session -- confirms the gap is holding.

complexity.reason: window-low check combined with session state from T19-14

candidates.name: OpenNearSessionExtreme
candidates.quote: Note how the open of the day was very close to the low of the day, which is a sign of strength, and trend from the open days that open within a few ticks of the low of the day often close within a few ticks of the high of the day.
candidates.description: The session's open still sits within a small distance of the session's running low (bull case) -- a sign this is a trend-from-the-open bull day likely to close near its high.

complexity.reason: needs the session's opening price and its running low/high tracked as state

notes: Brooks's own framing ('close to the low of the day') is technically only verifiable in hindsight at day's end; rewritten here as a real-time, in-session version (open still close to the running low so far).

candidates.name: NoClimaxBar
candidates.quote: No big climaxes appear.
candidates.description: Absence of a climax bar (an exceptionally large, extended trend bar signaling exhaustion) in the recent window -- a sign of an orderly, strong trend.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs a design decision on what qualifies as a 'climax' bar (extreme range + extended prior move + failure to follow through)

complexity.reason: Brooks does not give a numeric test for 'climax' here; a design decision is needed on how to define one before coding

candidates.name: FailedWedgeOrReversal
candidates.quote: Failed wedges and other failed reversals occur.
candidates.description: A wedge or other reversal pattern forms against the trend and then fails to reverse it (price breaks back through in the trend direction) -- a sign of trend strength.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs wedge/reversal pivot-pattern detection plus a subsequent failure/breakout-through test

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to identify a wedge/reversal pattern, then a follow-up test that it failed

candidates.name: NoTrendChannelOvershoot
candidates.quote: No significant trend channel line overshoots occur, and the minor ones result in only sideways corrections.
candidates.description: Price does not significantly overshoot the projected trend channel line, and any minor overshoot is followed by a sideways (not countertrend) correction.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs channel-line projection from swing pivots, plus classification of the post-overshoot correction as sideways vs countertrend

complexity.reason: needs trend-line/channel projection from pivots and a subsequent price-action classification

candidates.name: SidewaysCorrectionAfterTrendLineBreak
candidates.quote: The corrections after trend line breaks go sideways instead of countertrend.
candidates.description: After a trend-line break, the ensuing correction stays roughly flat rather than reversing hard against the trend -- a sign of strength.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs trend-line projection/break detection plus a range-vs-slope classification of the following N bars

complexity.reason: needs trend-line break detection plus classification of the subsequent price action

candidates.name: TwoLeggedPullbackRepeats
candidates.quote: Repeated two-legged pullbacks are setting up with trend entries.
candidates.description: Successive pullbacks against the trend each complete in exactly two legs before the trend resumes -- a recurring pattern that signals strength and sets up reliable with-trend entries.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs leg/swing counting per pullback, repeated across several pullbacks

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot/leg counting, and this concept is developed fully in chapter 20 (Two Legs)

notes: Expect this to merge with the two-legged-pullback primitives mined from 20_two_legs.txt.

candidates.name: TrendBreaksManyResistanceLevels
candidates.quote: The trend goes very far and breaks several resistance levels, like the moving average, prior swing highs, and trend lines, and each by many ticks.
candidates.description: Price decisively breaks multiple distinct resistance references (moving average, prior swing high, trend line) by more than a minimal margin -- a composite structural sign of a very strong trend.
candidates.pseudocode: // combines several sub-detections (EMA break, swing-high break, trend-line break) each by a minimum margin; needs a design decision on how many/which count as 'several'

complexity.reason: combines several hard sub-detections of heterogeneous reference types; needs a design decision on thresholds and counting before it can be coded

candidates.name: FailedCountertrendSpikeBecomesFlag
candidates.quote: Reversal attempts in the form of spikes against the trend have no follow-through, fail, and become flags in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: A strong countertrend spike fails to follow through (does not make a new extreme beyond a short window) and instead consolidates into a flag that resolves back in the prior trend's direction.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs spike/pattern detection plus a follow-through-failure test over a following window

complexity.reason: needs pattern recognition (spike) over a variable-length window plus a follow-through failure test

candidates.name: StrongTrendComposite
candidates.quote: The more of these signs that are present, the more you should focus on with-trend entries. ... once you realize that the market is in a strong trend, you don't need a setup to enter. You can enter anytime all day long at the market if you wish with a relatively small stop.
candidates.description: When a majority of the mechanizable signs-of-strength conditions above hold concurrently, classify the market as in a strong trend; in that state, permit setup-free with-trend entries at the market rather than requiring a specific pattern.
candidates.pseudocode: // count how many of the composed conditions are true and compare to a majority threshold; the 'enter at market once strong' policy is a separate design decision from the classification itself
candidates.book_order_type: market order once trend is classified strong, per Brooks; n/a for the classification itself

complexity.reason: requires a design decision on how many/which signs and thresholds constitute 'strong enough', plus a policy decision on setup-free market entries

notes: This is the chapter's unifying idea; kept as an Entry filter (not Switch) because it gates whether other with-trend entries can bypass their normal setup requirement rather than forcing flat.

rejected.quote: Few if any profitable countertrend trades are found.
rejected.reason: requires knowing the hypothetical profitability of countertrend trades that were not taken; not decidable from OHLCV bars or position state

rejected.quote: There is a sense of urgency. You find yourself waiting through countless bars for a good with-trend pullback and one never comes.
rejected.reason: subjective trader sentiment, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: In the strongest trends, the pullbacks usually have weak signal bars, making many traders not take them, and forcing traders to chase the market.
rejected.reason: descriptive correlation about trend strength causing weak signal bars, not an actionable if-then bar test; with-trend entries are already governed elsewhere regardless of signal-bar quality

rejected.quote: you might consider looking at the 3 minute chart for additional with-trend setups ... it is best to trade only off the 5 minute chart in a runaway trend.
rejected.reason: requires a second, faster-timeframe bar series that the engine does not have alongside the single configured bar series

rejected.quote: Stock traders would describe this bull channel up to yesterday's high as a crowded trade. Everyone who wanted to buy had already bought and there was no one left to buy.
rejected.reason: narrative market-psychology commentary, no bar-level test

chapter_summary: The chapter lists roughly two dozen characteristics common to strong trends (little pullback, trend-bar dominance, tiny tails, body gaps, measuring gaps, EMA gap-bar streaks, absence of climaxes/large bars/wedge failures/channel overshoots, multi-level breakouts, failed countertrend spikes) and argues that once enough of these are present a trader can enter with-trend at the market without waiting for a specific setup; most are mined here as their own is_filter Entry candidates, several graded hard/research because they need swing-pivot, trend-line, or pattern detection Brooks does not reduce to a number. The remainder of the chapter is two long worked chart examples (Figures 19.1-19.3) that narrate a full day bar-by-bar using concepts already defined elsewhere in the trilogy (H1/H2/L1/L2, signal bar, trend line break, wedge, moving-average gap bar, breakout pullback, failed breakout, double bottom, micro channel) -- these are not re-mined as new candidates, only reused, since they add no new mechanizable dimension beyond what those other chapters already define.
